question:
Consider the test class `TestMultilineAdjlistReadScenarios` in `networkx_qa/multiline_adjlist_parse_multiline_adjlist_m5_exceptions/files/testcase.py`. Run ALL 14 of its test methods (e.g. with `pytest networkx_qa/multiline_adjlist_parse_multiline_adjlist_m5_exceptions/files/testcase.py::TestMultilineAdjlistReadScenarios`). None of them calls the target directly; every method reaches it through `networkx.read_multiline_adjlist` (or `write_multiline_adjlist` followed by `read_multiline_adjlist`). The target function is `networkx.readwrite.multiline_adjlist.parse_multiline_adjlist`, defined in `networkx/readwrite/multiline_adjlist.py`.

Question: across the whole run (all invocations of the target in all 14 test methods together), how many times was an exception of each type observed in the target function's own frame?

Observation rule: an exception is observed in the target frame each time it becomes the active exception in that frame -- either because a statement executing in that frame raises it (an explicit `raise`, or a built-in operation/C-level call such as `int(...)`, `next(...)`, tuple unpacking or `**` unpacking raising it) or because it propagates into the frame from a Python callee (e.g. from `ast.literal_eval`). Every such observation counts once, whether the exception is later caught and swallowed in the target frame, converted into another exception, or escapes the frame. A `raise NewError(...) from err` inside an `except` block is a separate observation of the NEW exception (the original `err` was already counted when it was first observed). Exceptions raised and fully handled inside a callee that never reach the target frame do not count. The normal termination of a `for` loop over its iterable is not an exception observation. No exception in this run is re-raised by a bare `raise` in the target frame, so no single exception object is counted twice. Counts are totals over ALL invocations and ALL test methods (the same type observed in five methods contributes five).

Exception type naming: use bare `type(exc).__name__` for built-in exception classes (e.g. `KeyError`, never `builtins.KeyError`) and `module.QualName` for any other class (e.g. `networkx.exception.NetworkXError`). Use the concrete class of the exception object, not a base class.

Answer format: a JSON object with a single key `exception_type_counts`, whose value is a list of objects `{"count": <int>, "exception_type": <str>}`, one entry per distinct exception type observed at least once (types never observed are omitted; no entry has count 0). Sort the list by `exception_type` ascending (plain code-point string order); since each type appears once, no further tie-break is needed.
